extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and litigants involved in patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for the admissible evidence, burdens of proof, and kinds of proof required under common patent-infringement defenses (utility, abandonment, non-existence, illegality, joint/sole inventorship). Focuses on what establishes or rebuts each defense in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prima facie evidence of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is prima facie evidence in favor of the plaintiff on the issue of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the patent is prima facie evidence, the defendant must prove the uselessness of the invention beyond reasonable doubt. Ordinary testimony to show lack of utility comes from experts whose inspection satisfied them of its inutility and from practical mechanics who attempted to employ it and found it worthless. Courts generally do not reverse the Patent Office's decision that an invention is useful unless the defendant meets this burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence to prove lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony of experts inspecting the invention and practical mechanics who have attempted to use it and found it worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such testimony demonstrates the invention is mischievous or frivolous, the defense will be sustained. Plaintiff may rebut with experts of opposite opinions, practical mechanics with contrary experience, proof of extensive use, general effect on the art, or commercial success from which utility may be inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by defendant or licensee estops denial of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who is shown to have actually used the invention, whether wrongfully or under a license, or who has obtained a patent covering substantially the same art or article, is estopped from denying its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that the defendant used the invention or earlier obtained patents to substantially the same art is strong evidence against a claim of lack of utility; every doubt as to utility is resolved against a defendant who used the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prima facie evidence against abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent itself is prima facie evidence that there has been no abandonment at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant bears the burden to overcome this presumption by conclusive proof of dedication to the public. Abandonment may occur before application, during pendency, or after grant; the required certainty and weight of proof vary with timing (presumption against abandonment is stronger after application and strongest after issuance).

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes abandonment (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: No abandonment can take place unless the invention is complete and operative and available for immediate public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment is shown by acts or declarations manifesting an intention to abandon, by public use or sale with the inventor's acquiescence (see two-year rule), or by specific disclaimers or omissions in applications/claims. Mere omission to practice or to make application is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts showing abandonment before application
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntarily destroying the finished article without intending to rebuild it, distributing it asserting no effort would be made to patent it, or permitting its universal public use without objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncontradicted, such acts justify a jury finding of abandonment. The evidence must show the invention was made available to the public untrammelled by conditions which retain it under the inventor's control; tortious uses or sales without the inventor's knowledge are not proof of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale two-year rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment before the application may be shown by evidence of any public use or sale of the invention with the acquiescence of the inventor more than two years before the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of a single instance of such sale or use more than two years prior to application conclusively establishes abandonment and invalidates the patent. The use/sale must disclose a practical use for business purposes, observable by the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing application establishes non-abandonment at filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of the application for the patent proves irrefutably that the inventor did not then intend to abandon the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing is of greater weight than any doubtful prior acts of alleged dedication; declarations of the inventor that he did not intend to abandon cannot overcome inferences arising from his admitted conduct (e.g., acts showing acquiescence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment by application: disclaimers and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandonment by application may consist in a specific disclaimer of the invention, or in describing but omitting to insert it in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certified copy of the application containing the disclaimer is usually conclusive. Omission to claim a fully disclosed invention is regarded as conclusive dedication to the public unless the omitted invention is embraced in a new application or an amendment within a reasonable time. If suit is on a re-issue that supplies the defect, the issue is validity of the reissue, not abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable delay in seeking new patent may show abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in securing a new patent, after knowledge of a discrepancy between description and claim, may indicate unreasonable delay and support abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show inventor could have applied earlier and acquiesced in the disclosure of his unprotected invention for a period inconsistent with an original intention to claim it. Plaintiff may rebut only on the question of unreasonable delay except where his knowledge of insufficiency is derived from extraneous sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment after grant: high standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment after the patent is granted may be effected by overt acts or express declarations, or by neglect to act when action is evidently required; proof must be of the strongest and most conclusive character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every presumption is against abandonment after grant. Mere non-use is of no significance, but long continued acquiescence in its use by others or entire neglect to claim its advantages when the invention proved of great commercial value may satisfy a jury of abandonment. Evidence and counter-evidence of acts or omissions may be offered by the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-existence (Eighth defence): patent must correspond substantially with declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff's evidence and the defendant's evidence on this point is the patent itself: if it corresponds substantially with the averments in the declaration, the issue must be found for the plaintiff; if a substantial variance appears, the defendant is entitled to a judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient that the patent and its description agree in such formal parts as are essential to distinguish it from every other patent (date, title, number, grantee) and in the general tenor of its statements concerning the nature of the patented invention. Re-issues in equal divisions may support averments of multiple inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegality (Ninth defence): patent issued unlawfully if prerequisites unmet or jurisdiction exceeded
rubrics_metrics.description: The ninth defence asserts that the grant was unlawful because essential prerequisites were not fulfilled, or the grant exceeded the jurisdiction of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent affirmatively shows formal requirements were not heeded, no other evidence is necessary. When the patent asserts prerequisites were complied with, no contrary testimony can be offered unless the defendant claims fraud. When the patent is silent, issuance creates a presumption that prerequisites were observed and places burden on defendant to prove otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief formal defects: missing signatures and false oath
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief defects of which the law takes notice in an infringement action are the absence from the patent of necessary official signatures, and falsehood in the oath accompanying the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of necessary signatures is apparent on the face of the patent and is a fatal defect. A wilful false oath is a fraud which forfeits all the rights of the inventor; the oath is proved by a certified copy of the jurat, and its falsehood by evidence disclosing the true facts and the applicant's intent may be inferred from testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review and finality of Patent Office determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the Commissioner on matters within his exclusive jurisdiction (such as sufficiency of formal acts or allowance of extensions) are final and not subject to collateral attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision of the Commissioner allowing an extension or on formal matters is conclusive evidence as to the facts he is required to find in such administrative proceedings; collateral challenges are limited. However, some Commissioner determinations (e.g., abandonment of application) may not be conclusive in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint and several inventorship defects void patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint patent for a sole invention, and a sole patent for a joint invention, are alike void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joint application raises a presumption that applicants are joint inventors which can be overcome only by proof. The burden rests on the defendant to show by clear and unequivocal evidence that the patent improperly asserts sole inventorship when it was joint (or vice versa). Prior foreign patents do not change the burden of proof.
